days.reason: The day is dedicated to the archangel Michael and the service of angels. Matthew 18:10 is the central Bible text for this day in the church year, where Jesus confirms that the little ones have angels who see God's face. This is an explicit and unique connection.

The day marks the transition from celebration to repentance. Matthew 18:1-14 contains Jesus' call to repentance ('turn around and become like children'), humility, and a stern warning against letting sin lead to falling (hand, foot, eye). This is a classic Lenten text that encourages self-examination and cleaning up one's own life before Lent, which is the core of Shrove Tuesday themes.

The first Sunday in Lent deals with Jesus' temptation and the struggle against evil. Matthew 18:1-14, with its call to repentance ('turn around') and warning to remove what leads to falling (hand, foot, eye), is a very strong parallel to the theme of the start of Lent: cleaning up one's own life and fighting sin.

The day concerns Christ's return and the final judgment. The text contains strong eschatological warnings about 'the eternal fire' and 'hellfire' (vv. 8-9) as well as the promise that the Father does not want any of the little ones to be lost (v. 14). This gives a concrete picture of who will be judged and who will be saved, which is relevant for the theology of Judgment Sunday.

The day is dedicated to repentance, self-examination, and conversion. Matthew 18:15-35 provides the concrete procedure for conflict resolution and restoration in the church, as well as the parable of the unforgiving servant, which emphasizes the necessity of forgiving from the heart in response to God's infinite forgiveness. This is central to the practice of repentance and the healing of the community.

Matthew 18:10 is the central Bible text for this day in the church year, where Jesus warns against despising the little ones and confirms that their angels always see God's face. The text is explicitly mentioned in the description of the day.

The day concerns Christ's return and the final judgment. Matthew 18:1-14 contains Jesus' teaching on who are 'the least' in God's kingdom, the warning not to despise them, and the promise that the Father does not want any of these to be lost. This gives a concrete picture of who will be judged and who will be saved in judgment, which is central to the theology of Judgment Sunday.

The day is dedicated to repentance, self-examination, and conversion. Matthew 18:15-20 provides the concrete procedure for conflict resolution and restoration in the church (going to a brother alone, taking witnesses, telling the church), while the parable of the unforgiving servant (18:23-35) emphasizes the necessity of forgiving from the heart in response to God's infinite forgiveness. This is central to the practice of repentance.

_versions.reason: [major] The connection to Last Sunday is incorrect. Matthew 18 deals with humility, the value of children, the dangers of leading others astray, and forgiveness within the church. There is no explicit reference to Christ's return, the final judgment of the dead, or the imagery of judgment that characterizes Last Sunday (which is often linked to Matthew 25 or Revelation). Calling this "Last Sunday" based on "who will be judged" is a theological overinterpretation that does not hold up for day-tagging. The text is ethical teaching, not eschatological preaching about judgment.; [minor] Matthew 18:1-14 (especially verses 3-4 about turning and becoming like children, and verses 8-9 about removing what causes stumbling) is a classic text for Lent and especially for Shrove Sunday (which marks the transition into the season of repentance). The text concerning "repentance" (turning) and "self-examination" (removing hand or eye) fits perfectly with the theme of this day, which often focuses on cleaning up one's own life before Lent. This is a stronger connection than Last Sunday.; [minor] Matthew 18:19-20 ("where two or three are gathered in my name...") is a central text for Trinity Sunday in many church year traditions, as it points to God's presence in the community and the work of the Triune God within the church. Although it is not the only text, it is a strong liturgical connection that is missing.; [minor] Although the text deals with forgiveness and conflict resolution, "Day of Repentance and Prayer" is a specific day in the Norwegian church calendar (often in November) with a different liturgical profile than a general Lenten day. The text is more suitable for Lent generally or Shrove Sunday. Linking it to the Day of Repentance and Prayer is not wrong theologically, but liturgically, "Shrove Sunday" or "Lenten X" are usually the primary days for this text. I would still keep it as "secondary" if looking at the general theme, but "Shrove Sunday" is a better match for verses 1-14.

_versions.reason: [major] The connection to Trinity Sunday is incorrect. Matthew 18:19-20 concerns the power of prayer and God's presence in community, but contains no reference to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as a Trinity. Trinity Sunday requires a text that explicitly addresses the triune nature of God (e.g., Matt 28:19 or John 14-16). Using this text here is a theological overinterpretation that does not hold for specific day-tagging.; [minor] Although verses 1-14 are not an eschatological proclamation of judgment to the same degree as Matthew 25, the text contains references to 'the eternal fire', 'hellfire' and the warning not to let any of these little ones perish (v. 14). This has a strong ethical-eschatological dimension that can be linked to Judgment Sunday as a 'secondary' connection, especially in contrast to the pure Lenten theme. The previous version (score 6) had this as 'secondary', which is more balanced than linking it to Trinity Sunday.; [minor] Repentance and Prayer Day is a specific day in November in the Norwegian church calendar. Although the text deals with repentance, liturgically it is much better suited for Shrove Sunday (which marks the transition into Lent) or general Sundays during Lent. Linking the entire chapter (15-35) to Repentance and Prayer Day as 'secondary' is liturgically weaker than linking it to Shrove Sunday or days within Lent. The text is a classic Lenten passage.; [minor] Matthew 18:1-14 (especially v. 3-4 about turning around and becoming like children, and v. 8-9 about removing what causes stumbling) is a very strong text for the First Sunday of Lent. The theme of repentance and the struggle against sin fits perfectly into the beginning of Lent. This should be considered as a 'secondary' connection.
